extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of cultural criticism; educated public interested in literature, philosophy, and social critique
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying standards for what constitutes 'culture' and human perfection versus 'machinery' (wealth, industrialism, religion, etc.), as set out in a Victorian-era cultural-criticism essay. The rubric addresses how to judge social movements, institutions, and personal aims against an ideal of 'sweetness and light.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture as sweetness and light (criterion of perfection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture defines human perfection as a harmonious perfection in which 'the characters of beauty and intelligence are both present'—summed up as 'sweetness and light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay repeatedly asserts that the pursuit of 'sweetness and light' (beauty and intelligence) is the central aim of culture and the true ideal of human perfection. It contrasts this with other narrow ideals (e.g., wealth, moral rectitude) and insists culture works to make these qualities 'prevail' and to diffuse them widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject worship of machinery (wealth, population, industrialism, institutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth, population, bodily health, political and religious organizations are 'machinery' and must not be worshipped as ends in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate movements and institutions by whether they are treated as mere means ('machinery') toward higher ends. The text warns against treating industrialism, large families, or the franchise as inherently 'edifying'—such belief in machinery vulgarizes thought and should be criticized by culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental value of bodily health and vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily health and vigor are valuable only 'in reference to the services of the mind' and must be subordinated to spiritual and intellectual ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating exercise, eating, drinking, walking, riding as ultimate ends. Quoted authorities (Epictetus, Franklin) support doing bodily things 'merely by the way' so that 'the formation of the spirit and character must be our real concern.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture complements religious morality (beauty plus moral fibre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious organizations may cultivate moral self-conquest but their ideal is narrow; culture supplies the complementary ideal of beauty, harmony, and complete human perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing religious organizations, judge not only their success in moral self-discipline but also whether they foster 'sweetness and light' and a complete, harmonious human perfection. The essay argues religion's moral gains are insufficient without culture's aesthetic and intellectual completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate relative moral satisfaction with complete spiritual perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: The inward peace from partial moral victories (resisting obvious animal faults) is not the same as absolute inward peace approaching complete spiritual perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of using the exalted language of complete perfection to describe incomplete moral states; such misuse obscures shortcomings. Religious rhetoric often encourages this conflation and should be critically examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique necessary movements for their present human cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture may admit the necessity of movements (e.g., industrialism, Puritanism) for the future, but must criticize how passing generations are 'sacrificed' to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating policies or social trends, balance their long-term justification against the immediate suffering or vulgarization they impose on current generations. Culture congratulates the future but insists present costs be acknowledged and criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to fanaticism and system-making (Jacobinism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture resists Jacobinism's fierceness and addiction to abstract systems and the imposition of a single 'Rabbi' (leader/solution); it favors continual seeking and skepticism of dogma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blind allegiance to abstract doctrines or charismatic system-makers. Culture values passing on from any single 'Rabbi' and critiques the tendency to make a thinker or system stand for perfection, urging ongoing critical inquiry instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible, merciful judgment of persons; severe judgment of actions
rubrics_metrics.description: In politics and social critique the cultured temper combines severe judgment of actions with indulgence for persons' circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture's political stance is not vindictive or fanatical; it exercises 'indulgence proper to culture' by considering circumstances and showing mercy to persons while firmly criticizing harmful actions and tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanize and diffuse the best knowledge (method of educating masses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture seeks to make 'the best that has been thought and known in the world current everywhere' by humanizing knowledge—divesting it of harshness, exclusiveness, and professional abstraction—rather than teaching down with ready-made judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or evaluating educational or popularizing work, aim to keep content genuinely excellent ('the best knowledge') while making it accessible and humanized. Do not condescend or simplify into mere watchwords; the goal is diffusion without debasement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social idea: apostles of equality through culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of culture are 'the true apostles of equality' because they work to spread sweetness and light across society and abolish class-based exclusivity of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure cultural activity by its success in expanding access to genuine thought and taste across classes. The social aim is broad permeation of real thought and beauty, producing national glows of life and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge organizations by the life they image and produce
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess the value of religious or political organizations, look 'at the life imaged' in their organs (e.g., newspapers), the habits and pleasures they cultivate, and whether those lives approximate complete human perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical evaluation requires examining concrete manifestations—literature, printed organs, public life—rather than only official doctrines. If an organization's everyday life is 'unlovely' or 'incomplete,' that undermines its claim to promote perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote national permeation of 'real' thought and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture desires a broad national diffusion where 'the whole of society is in the fullest measure permeated by thought, sensible to beauty, intelligent and alive,' but insists the thought and beauty be real, not diluted popular substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects aimed at mass cultural improvement should prioritize authenticity: 'real thought and real beauty.' Beware popular literature or indoctrination that adapts ideas to perceived inferior tastes rather than raising general standards through genuine humanized excellence.
